title: Minimal Group Allocation Laboratory
summary: The learner is sorted into an arbitrary fictional category on a basis the page immediately admits is meaningless, then allocates symbolic points between one anonymous member of each category, six times. Every option prints its own arithmetic, so the option that gives the learner's own category fewer points in exchange for a larger lead is visible rather than disguised. The same six allocations can then be run in a world where the learner's category already holds four times as much, and in one where it holds a quarter - which makes visible the thing a strategy profile cannot record, that an identical choice creates an inequality in one world and widens an existing one in another.
learningObjectives: Distinguish four allocation strategies and say what each one reveals about the allocator's goal.
Explain why choosing maximum difference over maximum ingroup gain is the finding that no self-interest account reaches.
Describe what social identity theory means by positive distinctiveness and why it is a comparative claim.
State why an allocation pattern between two invented categories is not an explanation of prejudice or of structural inequality.
Judge which conclusions this kind of evidence supports, partly supports and does not support.
interactionTypes: strategy profile chart with full text equivalent
privacy: Allocations are held in the browser tab only, are used solely to draw the profile in front of the learner, and are discarded when the page is left; nothing is saved, stored or transmitted, and no score or judgement about any person is produced.
accessibilityNotes: Nothing is timed. Every allocation option is a native radio in a labelled fieldset and prints its full arithmetic - points to each side, total, and signed difference - in text, so no choice depends on reading the chart or on colour. The strategy chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a sentence naming all four counts and the running totals; the largest-lead bar is drawn differently but is also named in words. The comparison table is a real table with row headers and a scroll wrapper. The progress checklist marks each item met or not yet in text as well as by marker. Changes, including the category assignment and every recorded allocation, are announced through the shell's polite live region. Headings run h1 to h5 without skipping, focus moves to the laboratory heading when it opens, targets are at least 2.75rem, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
readmeTopic: Sorted into an invented category, allocating points to strangers - and the option that costs your own side points to buy a bigger lead
simulationNotes: The two categories (Kestrels and Wrens), the sorting question and all six allocation matrices are original and authored for teaching; no published matrix, instruction set or dataset is reproduced. In every matrix the largest-lead option gives the learner's own category fewer points than the own-group-most option does (19 against 25, 15 against 20, 22 against 29, 13 against 18, 18 against 24, 16 against 22), which is what makes the choice between them diagnostic, and the largest-total option always has the highest sum. No simulated respondents are involved and no distribution of choices is modelled: the profile shown is only the learner's own six decisions. The three starting positions - 100 against 100, 400 against 100, 100 against 400 - are this tool's own addition rather than part of the classic paradigm, and are stipulated rather than earned. The worked example runs the pattern fair, largest lead, fair, own group most, largest lead, fair in the equal and already-ahead conditions, producing three fair, no largest-total, one own-group-most and two largest-lead allocations in each, a gap moving from +0 to +25 in the equal condition and from +300 to +325 in the already-ahead condition. Those two rows show the same strategy profile doing two different things, which is the point the comparison table exists to make.
